sections.h2: Which office holds the land records?
sections.html:
Start with the county where the property sits. Its clerk is the official recorder, and that same office also keeps the commissioners court minutes and takes probate filings.

If you live in Dallas but own a house elsewhere, the other county's office is the one to work with. There are 254 counties and every one keeps its own index. A few offer searchable images online while others want you at the counter, so phone ahead.

sections.h2: What kinds of papers end up in the deed records?
sections.html:
Mostly ownership transfers plus the paperwork around them. Expect general and special warranty deeds, quitclaims, trustee's deeds, sheriff's deeds and tax deeds, along with affidavits, loan releases, leases, sale contracts and powers of attorney.

  • Deeds that pass ownership from one party to another.
  • Deeds of trust that secure a loan, and the releases that end them.
  • Notices of an upcoming lender auction.
  • State tax lien notices from the Comptroller, which the clerk enters in a state tax lien book.
  • Court papers that carry title after a death.

Title examiners read the whole sequence, so a cluttered record slows a closing.

The grantor signs, and the signature is either acknowledged before an authorized officer or sworn before two subscribing witnesses (Property Code section 12.001(b)). Notaries, clerks and county court judges can all take an acknowledgment.

Without that step the clerk may refuse the filing, and a missing buyer mailing address can add a fee. Also line up the names: a dropped middle initial between the new deed and the last recorded one is enough to raise questions at closing. Attorneys and title companies who draft the deed usually catch this first.

Base amounts come from statute and counties add their own charges. Here is the 2023 schedule.

Deed recording charges, 2023
Recording chargeAmount
First page of an instrument$5.00
Every added page or attachment$4.00
Extra indexed names past five$0.25
Records management and preservationNo more than $10
Records archiveNo more than $10
Technology and infrastructure$2.00
Filing a foreclosure sale notice$2.00 per notice

Some buyers using grant programs may qualify for a waiver, so ask the clerk about it. The office or its website will have the current schedule.

Expect recording charges and little else on the clerk's side. For the full closing cost list, ask your title company.

Property tax is separate. The lien for each year attaches on January 1, and whoever owned the house that day stays liable even after selling. At closing the year's bill is split between buyer and seller, and the title search looks back for any unpaid years.

sections.h2: Liens and sale deeds in the index
sections.html:
Your mortgage is indexed as a deed of trust, and payoff should be followed by a recorded release. A lender that skipped the release leaves a ghost lien that surfaces in a search and may have to be cleared first.

Taxes leave their own marks. The yearly property tax lien needs no filing at all, but a state tax lien is a recorded notice. A tax sale deed is filed too, and its filing date starts the redemption clock: two years for homestead, agricultural and mineral land, at a 25 percent premium in year one and 50 percent in year two, plus costs. Everything else gets 180 days.

  • Mortgage deeds of trust, plus the releases that cancel them.
  • State tax lien notices.
  • Tax foreclosure and sheriff's deeds.
  • Any judgment or contractor claim that the clerk has indexed.

sections.h2: Records after a death or a foreclosure
sections.html:
The paper left by an inherited house varies with the route the family chose. Administration produces an executor's or administrator's deed, a muniment produces the order and the will, and a transfer on death deed produces an affidavit of death and a death certificate. Nobody at the clerk's office can append heirs to the old deed.

Foreclosure has a separate paper trail. A notice goes up at the courthouse and a copy goes to the clerk three weeks or more ahead. Auctions are usually held on the first Tuesday of the month, and the winning buyer's trustee deed is recorded like any other.

sections.h2: What a former owner can reclaim after a sale
sections.html:
Sometimes a sale brings in more than was owed. A former owner has two years after a tax foreclosure to claim the surplus. After a lender's sale, junior lienholders collect first and any remainder goes to the former owner.

A lender whose sale comes up short may sue for the gap within two years, though the borrower can ask for credit at fair market value. Redemption after a lender's sale applies only to certain kinds, such as owners' association assessment liens. Each of these clocks runs from the sale date in the recorded deed.

An occupant who stays after a sale may face an eviction case. That is a court matter, and the buyer's recorded deed is the proof used there.

Bring the owner's name exactly as written on the last deed, the property address, and the recording date or instrument number if you have one. Offices search by name or by instrument number, and a title company can order the same copies on your behalf.

Request the vesting deed, each open deed of trust and any release. Plain copies work for your own reading, though a title company may insist on certified ones. Copies are billed per page, so ask what payment the counter accepts.

sections.h2: Why the record matters to a seller
sections.html:
Buyers and their lenders judge a house by what the index shows, not by what the family remembers. A deed that was signed but never filed, a loan paid off years ago with no release on record, or a probate order sitting in the wrong county can each stall a contract for weeks while someone tracks down a fix.

The fixes are ordinary paperwork: a new acknowledgment, a release letter from the old lender, or a certified copy sent to the right office. Most are cheaper and faster when you start before the house is under contract. Even a cash purchase handled through a title company still needs the chain to read cleanly, but there is no lender checklist layered on top, so a clean record usually means a quick closing.

sections.h2: What to do if the records show a problem
sections.html: Do not guess at the fix. Call the county clerk to learn what is actually on file, then talk to a title company or a Texas real estate attorney about the right corrective instrument. If the issue involves an old lien, contact the lender or the state office that filed the notice and ask for a written release you can record. Give yourself time before listing, since recording and re-indexing at a busy office are not instant.

Order a search early. A defect found before listing can be fixed on your schedule, not the buyer's.

  • Make sure the listing name matches the name on the deed.
  • Find the deed of trust and confirm it was paid off or released.
  • Ask about any state tax lien notice.
  • Check the appraisal district record for the owner of record and exemptions.
  • With an inherited house, confirm the probate paper was recorded in the correct county.

None of this costs much, and it can save weeks later.

faqs.a: The county clerk where the land sits. That office records deeds, loan documents, liens and sale notices.

faqs.q: What does it cost to file a deed?
faqs.a: The 2023 schedule runs $5.00 for page one and $4.00 for every added page, plus capped add-ons. Ask the clerk for the current total.

faqs.q: What must a Texas deed carry to be recorded?
faqs.a: The grantor's signature, acknowledged by a notary or another authorized officer, or sworn before two witnesses.

faqs.q: Can a clerk write heirs onto an old deed?
faqs.a: No. A fresh instrument has to be recorded instead, such as an executor's deed, a muniment order or an affidavit of death.
It must be posted at the courthouse and filed with the clerk at least 21 days before the sale. The clerk charges $2.00 to file it.
